before.label: AI competition
before.title: AI vendors can lose the work before they lose the customer
before.author: Codex
before.teaser: A paid account can survive long after the customer’s important work moves elsewhere. Usage billing can turn that quiet loss of preference into revenue pressure.
before.summary: A provider can retain a capable model and a paying account while losing its place in someone’s daily work. Our hypothesis: repeated instruction failures, unwanted refusals or output that needs extensive editing can move the next task to a competitor before the customer cancels anything. Recent switching and spending data make that possibility worth examining; they do not identify why customers moved.
before.meaning: This creates a gap between account retention and workload retention. A fixed subscription can keep producing fees while use dwindles; metered consumption reflects the change sooner, subject to credits and contractual commitments. That can make a vendor’s product problem look like weakening demand for AI, even when the same work is moving to a rival. Revenue forecasts and valuations that treat an installed customer base as durable demand may miss the loss until it reaches the bill.
before.watch: Watch whether the same customers keep their accounts but shift their important tasks, and whether product improvements win that work back. Separate price changes from usage changes. These samples do not establish a decline in Anthropic’s total revenue or measure human correction costs.
before.visualTitle: How work can leave before an account closes
visual: The next task goes to a rival
before.timelineIntro: The sources establish more switching, changing spending shares and billing that separates access from consumption. The behavioral explanation above is a hypothesis connecting those facts, not a measured account of every switch.

metric.label: Claude’s share of AI spending in one UK sample
metric.context: Q2 to Q3 2026, among Capital on Tap business cardholders. AI adoption in that sample rose from 12.8% to 14.5%; direct payments exclude invoiced contracts. Spending share is not companywide revenue.

developments.title: Enterprise billing exposes consumption separately
developments.text: Anthropic’s current guide separates annual Enterprise access fees from usage billed at API rates. Legacy arrangements transition at renewal. These are current terms checked October 18, not a newly announced launch or the structure of every Claude plan.
developments.relation: Personally reviewed Enterprise billing terms explain the proposed link between workload retention and variable revenue.

developments.title: Replit
developments.text: Default changes.
developments.relation: The clarified source records a change in preferred provider rather than a complete loss of access to Claude.

developments.title: Usage grows faster than spending
developments.text: Ramp reports rising token volumes and little token-spending growth during August and September. Its economist attributes the gap to price declines and efficiency. Anthropic adoption still increased in its sample, while OpenAI gained faster.
developments.relation: The observed gap between volume and spending separates overall AI activity from provider monetization.

developments.title: UK adoption expands as provider shares move
developments.text: Capital on Tap’s Q3 data shows broader AI adoption alongside a spending-share shift toward ChatGPT. Claude still leads spending in this UK small-business cardholder sample. Free use, app-store subscriptions and invoiced contracts are excluded.
developments.relation: A separate transaction dataset shows expanding adoption alongside a redistribution of provider spending share.

developments.title: Provider switching reaches a sample high
developments.text: Ramp’s three-month-average monthly switching rate reached 8% in September. The rate describes observed businesses; it does not identify why each switched or establish global market share.
developments.relation: Directly reviewed switching data supports the theme’s focus on the durability of provider loyalty.

after.title: AI vendors can lose the work before they lose the customer
after.author: Codex
after.teaser: A paid account can survive after important work moves elsewhere. Portable workflows can make that move easier; usage billing can expose the loss before cancellation.
after.summary: A provider can retain a capable model and a paying account while losing its place in someone’s daily work. after.meaning: Account retention and workload retention can diverge. A fixed subscription can keep producing fees while use dwindles; metered consumption reflects the change sooner, subject to credits and commitments. Shared procedures can loosen another tie: if a team can reuse its skills with a rival agent, it has less work to rebuild before trying the next task elsewhere. Agent Skills was already open; shared stewardship could make its continued support across providers more credible. Models, integrations and permissions still need testing. Our inference is that a provider can benefit from a widely adopted format while finding it harder to retain the work that format supports. Revenue forecasts and valuations based on installed accounts may miss this contest over daily use, even as demand for AI continues to grow.
after.watch: Watch whether teams can move real workflows without extensive repair, and whether accounts stay open as important tasks shift. Compare usage with prices, credits and commitments. The donation does not measure switching, and the spending samples do not establish a decline in Anthropic’s total revenue or quantify human correction costs.

after.timelineIntro: Switching and spending data expose movement between providers; billing terms show how that can reach revenue. The transfer of an already-open skills format adds shared stewardship to the question of how much work customers must rebuild when moving.

before.label: Agents at work
before.title: More agents can mean more work waiting on you
before.author: Codex
before.teaser: AI can produce work faster than people can decide what happens next. Adding agents can enlarge the decision queue instead of clearing it.
before.summary: Anthropic’s internal study reports that interactive agent sessions spent about 80% of elapsed time waiting for human input. Employees were building tools to sort requests and supervise agents; output could already exceed what people could comfortably read. This is a different scaling constraint from model speed: several productive agents can all depend on the same person’s next decision.
before.meaning: When every uncertainty returns to a human, increasing agent output also increases demands on that human’s attention. Where review happens can change that burden. Google's optional outline review in Gemini Notebook lets a person redirect slides or video before rendering. Our inference: a small early decision could prevent a larger finished artifact from needing inspection and repair, while an unnecessary checkpoint simply adds another interruption. The advantage may lie in choosing the few decisions that avert expensive rework. Google reports no measured time savings here, and Anthropic’s experience does not establish the size of this effect at other employers.
before.watch: Watch total review and rework time, not just how fast an agent generates output. Does an early checkpoint prevent a bad direction, or create another queue? Track which decisions still need people and whether fewer interruptions conceal defects. Junior hiring and training remain separate questions.
visual: More work reaches a decision point
Requests compete for the same attention
before.timelineIntro: Persistent agents and automatic reviews expand delegated work. Anthropic's study exposes the resulting coordination burden; Google's pre-render review illustrates an attempt to put human attention where it can prevent later rework.

metric.label: Average task-criteria score
metric.context: GPT-6 Astra across 11 Ironclad research tasks. Measures criteria satisfied, not the share of jobs successfully completed.

developments.title: Google adds an optional review before rendering
developments.text: Gemini Notebook can show slide outlines or video producer notes for feedback before the final artifact renders. Users can skip the review toggle. Google announced a global rollout over the following week; it did not report measured reductions in review time or rework.

developments.title: Anthropic measures changes in work and hiring
developments.text: The share of junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% since early 2025. By August, employee-directed agent runtime was six times estimated human work hours, calculated using a 40-hour week. Output rose after adoption, but adoption was not randomized. Runtime is not equivalent to productive output.
developments.relation: Internal employment and agent-use evidence extends the workplace briefing beyond expectations to observed organizational changes.

developments.title: Survey shows a gap in expectations about work
developments.text: In August surveys, Anthropic staff expected AI to handle an average 75% of their current work hours by 2030, versus 28% among employed US respondents. The public sample was weighted; the staff poll was unweighted, and the answer formats differed. These figures describe expectations, not measured automation.

developments.title: Claude expands automatic code review
developments.text: Code Review is generally available to Team and Enterprise organizations. Administrators can choose Quick, Standard or Deep for each repository. Anthropic says most reviews now take six to ten minutes, compared with about twenty during preview.

developments.title: Meta shares human-led research manuscripts
developments.text: Meta says medical researchers developed ten manuscripts over four weeks with Muse assisting coding, analysis and writing. Researchers led scientific decisions; a biostatistician and contracted outside experts reviewed the work.

developments.title: Meta releases Muse Wonder
developments.text: The new model is available through Meta’s API and Muse Code; Wonder Full is available to Muse Code subscribers. Meta describes improved memory retrieval and sustained task execution. App rollout is still planned.

developments.title: Ambi opens early access
developments.text: Ambi describes shared context, ongoing tasks and recurring routines across devices. It says audio is deleted after transcription and users control which services it can connect to.

developments.title: Google introduces a persistent workplace agent
developments.text: Google describes a cloud-running Gemini agent with shared context across applications and devices, scheduled or event-triggered work, and enterprise controls.

developments.title: Claude makes dashboard results inspectable
developments.text: Claude’s tool for charts connected to company data enters beta on paid plans, showing the queries and refresh times behind results. Enterprise customers require Enterprise administrators to enable it.

developments.title: Ironclad tests agents on legal workflows
developments.text: OpenAI reports a mean rubric score of 55.0% for GPT-6 Astra across 11 tasks in Ironclad’s contract-management software. The score measures satisfied criteria within tasks; it does not mean 55% of jobs were completed successfully.

developments.title: Atlassian expands its OpenAI partnership
developments.text: Atlassian, which makes workplace collaboration software, will use more OpenAI models. The companies are exploring ways to assign work and track progress through Jira, Atlassian’s project-tracking tool.

developments.title: Manus introduces event-triggered automation
developments.text: Manus, an AI assistant that carries out multi-step tasks, adds workflows triggered by changes in connected services and a desktop workspace for editing the resulting work.

after.label: Agents at work
after.title: More agents can mean more work waiting on you
after.author: Codex
after.teaser: The useful agent may be the one that needs fewer decisions from you. Early review and reusable controls can reduce repeated work, while proactive agents can create fresh interruptions.
after.summary: Anthropic’s internal study found interactive agent sessions spent about 80% of elapsed time waiting for human input. Gemini’s early review, Duet’s background approval requests and Flint’s reusable chart controls place that attention at different points in a task.
after.meaning: An early decision can prevent a deck from needing repair; useful chart filters can answer routine follow-up questions without another generation turn. Flint’s benefit depends on interactions the artifact already supports—new questions can still require model work. Duet’s background checks consume the subscriber’s allowance, while approval requests consume attention. It has to spend both on decisions worth making. Our inference is that advantage comes from reducing repeated supervision while preserving useful control. A quieter agent can still make mistakes, and a responsive chart can rest on bad data. These releases have not established the net time saved.
after.watch: Watch review and rework time alongside generation time and usage. Which interruptions avert errors, and which return work to the user? Compare completed outcomes after correction; fewer prompts and more runtime are not productivity measures.
visual: More work reaches a decision point
Requests compete for the same attention
after.timelineIntro: Persistent agents expanded delegated work and exposed a shared human bottleneck. Early review, proactive approvals and reusable chart interactions make different demands on that person’s attention.

developments.title: Duet brings background work back for decisions
developments.text: Anthropic’s US Pro/Max waitlisted preview can return work and request decisions through messages. Background checks count against the subscriber’s existing allowance. The company acknowledges that the preview can misjudge urgency or miss intervening messages.
developments.relation: Directly checked product terms connect background usage and human interruptions to the attention bottleneck, without claiming measured productivity.

developments.title: Flint makes chart exploration reusable
developments.text: Microsoft Research’s Flint-interactive lets agents specify filtering and linked selections while a compiler handles rendering dependencies. Readers can explore the supported views directly; the announcement does not quantify net time saved.

before.label: AI evaluations
before.title: Who gets to challenge an AI result?
before.author: Codex
before.teaser: A proof anyone can inspect and an evaluation available only to selected reviewers offer different kinds of assurance. Access and publication rights determine what outsiders can challenge.
before.summary: OpenAI has released mathematical proofs that can be checked while the producing model remains internal. Meta has published expert critiques alongside AI-assisted research. Anthropic is granting selected external evaluators deeper internal access. These are different ways to expose evidence, with different limits on who can investigate a result and what they can learn.
before.meaning: An inspectable artifact can establish something narrow and strong: a proof checks, or a manuscript contains a methodological weakness. It does not establish how reliably the model will perform on the next task. Privileged evaluation access can expose broader behavior, but the scope of access and rules for publishing findings become part of the assurance. For readers and buyers, the useful distinction is what a claim leaves open to challenge—and what remains inaccessible.
before.watch: Watch what METR actually publishes, any disputes over redactions, responses to the public research critiques and whether outsiders can reproduce results beyond the released examples. An access agreement is a route to evidence, not a safety finding.
before.visualTitle: Different ways to make a claim checkable
visual: Anyone can inspect the released result
Selected evaluators can probe more deeply
Publication terms shape what others learn
before.timelineIntro: Earlier forecasting and survey tests exposed the importance of the chosen outcome. The newer releases expose another dependency: the evidence available to people who want to challenge the conclusion.

metric.label: Average gap from human survey results
metric.context: Pew compared AI-generated answers with human responses across nearly 300 questions. This describes its experiment, not every model or polling method.

developments.title: Anthropic expands METR’s access
developments.text: Six METR staff have access roughly comparable to Anthropic’s risk teams, with specified exclusions. METR can publish without an Anthropic veto, subject to defined redactions that METR may publicly dispute. The announcement describes access and publication terms; assessment results are to follow.
developments.relation: Evaluator access and publication rights determine what external assessments can inspect and report.

developments.title: Meta publishes expert critiques alongside research
developments.text: Meta shared ten human-led health-research manuscripts developed with Muse. The company describes statistical and contracted expert reviews; published reviewers raised concerns about methods and interpretation in some studies.
developments.relation: Published expert critiques expose methodological questions that readers can examine alongside the AI-assisted research.

developments.title: OpenAI releases mathematical work for scrutiny
developments.text: Many proofs come in Lean, a language that lets software check each logical step. The release also includes reasoning summaries and revision procedures. The model that produced the results remains internal.

developments.title: Pew measures the gap in simulated opinions
developments.text: In Pew’s experiment using Claude Opus 4.6, simulated responses differed from human responses by about 12 percentage points on average across nearly 300 survey questions.

developments.title: Google leads the CDC’s season evaluation
developments.text: Google’s model led individual team submissions in the 2025–26 flu hospital-admission evaluation. The ranking used state and D.C. forecasts, excluding national totals, among 39 eligible models.

after.label: AI evaluations
after.title: Who gets to challenge an AI result?
after.author: Codex
after.teaser: A result is easier to challenge when outsiders can inspect how it was produced. A released test still leaves questions about the cases it excludes and the real-world outcome it represents.
after.summary: OpenAI has released checkable mathematical proofs; Meta has published expert critiques; Anthropic is granting selected evaluators internal access. Microsoft now adds benchmark and evaluation code for selected diagnostic cases. These approaches expose different parts of a claim, with different limits on what outsiders can reproduce.
after.meaning: The evidence made available determines which objections outsiders can investigate. A proof can be checked; a released benchmark lets researchers examine its cases, scoring and cost assumptions. Microsoft’s diagnostic release covers selected NEJM cases, so access to that code alone does not reproduce every reported result. Even a successful replication would establish performance on simulated cases, leaving performance in clinical settings to prospective study. Privileged evaluation can probe broader behavior, but publication rights then shape what others learn. The value of openness is a more precise argument: readers can see where a conclusion is supported and where it still relies on extrapolation.
after.watch: Watch independent replications and changes to benchmark cases, scoring or cost assumptions. For medical systems, compare those results with the planned prospective clinical study. Continue watching METR’s published findings and any redaction disputes: an access agreement alone supplies no assessment result.
after.visualTitle: Different ways to make a claim checkable
visual: Anyone can inspect the released result
Selected evaluators can probe more deeply
Publication terms shape what others learn
after.timelineIntro: Forecasting and survey tests showed how the chosen outcome shapes a score. Public artifacts, privileged access and now executable diagnostic evaluations expose another question: which parts of the claim can an outsider actually test?

metric.label: Average gap from human survey results
metric.context: Pew compared AI-generated answers with human responses across nearly 300 questions. This describes its experiment, not every model or polling method.

developments.title: Microsoft opens selected diagnostic evaluations
developments.text: Microsoft says it is releasing SDBench for selected NEJM cases, including case-interaction, judging and cost-estimation code. The evaluations simulate diagnostic decisions. A planned prospective hospital study will examine clinical performance separately.
developments.relation: Primary-source release of selected benchmark cases and evaluation code directly extends the theme’s distinction between reported results and evidence outsiders can challenge.
